newsitem.title: HONG KONG: S'pore opposition leader urges HK press to fight.
newsitem.headline: S'pore opposition leader urges HK press to fight.

text.p: Prominent Singapore opposition politician Chee Soon Juan urged Hong Kong journalists on Friday to fight to preserve press freedom after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.

"My only suggestion to the Hong Kong press is to fight and fight like hell," said Chee, secretary-general of the Singapore Democratic Party, who lost in his bid for a parliamentary seat in Singapore's general election in January.

Chee, addressing a luncheon at the Hong Kong Foreign Correspondents' Club, also said he doubted if it would be possible for governments anywhere else in the world to exercise the kind of control over the media seen in Singapore.
"Singapore, people forget, is just an island," he said.
"While we're able to really control society as the People's Action Party (PAP) has been controlling Singapore, the island, it's a lot harder to try to do the same in any other country."
Singapore's media is tightly regulated. Newspapers tend to closely reflect the view of the rulng party and opponents of the government often complain they get inadequate media access.

Hong Kong, a British colony of over 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule from July 1 and while it has been promised a high degree of self-rule for a further 50 years, fears are mounting that its freewheeling and democratic ways would be stifled.

Hong Kong's post-colonial constitution guarantees Hong Kong can maintain its current freedoms but senior Chinese officials in the past have warned the Hong Kong press against advocating independence for Hong Kong or Taiwan.
Chee also expressed disappointment with results of the Singapore poll where the ruling PAP won 65 percent of the vote and all but two seats.

A key strategy used in PAP's campaign platform was a warning to voters that constituencies that did not support the party would lose out on a multi-billion dollar programme to renovate housing estates.
"Results of the recent polls boil down to one fact. That Singaporeans are willing to mortgage our freedoms for material gain and...sooner or later, we will pay the price," Chee said.
"With all the control of information, thinking has become a rare activity in Singapore and thinkers an endangered species."
